scenes.narration: The datetime module has three main tools. A date holds a year, a month and a day. A datetime also holds hours, minutes and seconds. A timedelta is a length of time, such as thirty days. You can add it to a date. You also get one when you subtract two dates. To turn a date into text, use strftime, with a format string such as percent d percent B. To read text into a date, use strptime, with the same type of format. Think of a wall calendar and a pocket watch, both able to count forward.

code.source:
from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

d = date(2025, 1, 15)
print(d)
print(d.year, d.month, d.day)
print(d.strftime("%d %B %Y"))
print(d.strftime("%A"))
later = d + timedelta(days=30)
print(later)
print((later - d).days)

scenes.onScreen: The names d and later tied to two separate date objects; adding a timedelta builds a new one
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. The name d is tied to one date object. The name later is tied to a different date object. Adding a timedelta did not change d. Dates are immutable. Every calculation builds a new date, and the old one stays exactly as it was.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] Import datetime. [HL 3] A date and time, written as text. [HL 4] Strptime reads the text, using a format that matches it exactly. Year, month, day, hour, minute. [HL 5] Now the parts are numbers. Eighteen thirty. [HL 6] Strftime writes it back, in twelve hour style. Six thirty PM. [HL 7] A second datetime, built from numbers. [HL 8] Subtract, and we get a timedelta. One hour, thirty minutes. [HL 9] And datetimes compare with less than. True.

code.source:
from datetime import datetime

text = "2025-03-09 18:30"
t = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
print(t.hour, t.minute)
print(t.strftime("%I:%M %p"))
end = datetime(2025, 3, 9, 20, 0)
print(end - t)
print(t < end)

shorts.script: A date holds a year, a month and a day. A datetime holds a time as well, hours, minutes and seconds. Create one with numbers, such as date, twenty twenty five, one, fifteen. Printing gives a tidy year, month, day. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Dates are objects.

shorts.title: timedelta
shorts.hook: "A timedelta is a length of time."
shorts.script: A timedelta is a length of time. Add timedelta of thirty days to a date, and you get a later date. Subtract two dates, and you get a timedelta, with a days attribute. Python handles months and leap years for you. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python counts days for you.

shorts.title: strftime
shorts.script: Strftime turns a date into text. Percent d is the day. Percent B is the month name. Percent Y is the year. Percent A is the weekday. Mix them, and you can write the date in any style you like. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: strftime writes text.

shorts.title: strptime
shorts.script: Strptime does the opposite. It reads text into a datetime, using a format that must match exactly. Slashes in the text need slashes in the format. A mismatch raises a value error, time data does not match format. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
